lead: A lattice is a poset in which every pair has a join and a meet. The order definition forces a fixed set of identities: idempotent, commutative, associative and absorption laws. These laws let you simplify expressions without drawing the Hasse diagram. A sublattice is a nonempty subset that is closed under both join and meet, with the order inherited from the parent lattice. Closure tests decide whether a smaller set of divisors, states or bit patterns is a valid lattice in its own right; checking only one operation is a common mistake.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for the poset definition and the join and meet operations.

blocks.text: Take a lattice L with order ≤. For a,b∈L, a∨b is the least element that is ≥ both a and b; a∧b is the greatest element that is ≤ both. The order therefore forces four families of identities.

Idempotent and commutative follow from sets. The set {a,a} is just {a}, so its least upper bound and greatest lower bound are both a. The set {a,b} equals {b,a}, so the order of the inputs cannot change the answer.

Associative: (a∨b)∨c and a∨(b∨c) are both the least upper bound of {a,b,c}; the same set argument gives the meet law. Absorption: a∧b≤a, so a is an upper bound of a and a∧b. Every upper bound u of those two has u≥a, hence a is the least such upper bound. This proves a∨(a∧b)=a. Swap ∨ with ∧ and reverse ≤ to get the dual law a∧(a∨b)=a.
a ∨ (a ∧ b) = a,    a ∧ (a ∨ b) = a
blocks.where: a and b are elements of L; the second identity is the dual of the first, obtained by swapping ∨ with ∧.

blocks.text: Monotonicity says order survives when the same c is joined or met on both sides. If a≤b then the join with c and the meet with c also satisfy the same direction.
a ≤ b  implies  a∨c ≤ b∨c  and  a∧c ≤ b∧c
blocks.where: a,b,c∈L; ∨ is join and ∧ is meet.

blocks.text: For join, b∨c is ≥b≥a and ≥c, so it is an upper bound of a and c. The least upper bound a∨c is therefore ≤b∨c. For meet, a∧c≤a≤b and a∧c≤c, so a∧c is a lower bound of b and c. The greatest lower bound b∧c is therefore ≥a∧c.

Use monotonicity when a value is replaced by a larger one in a merge point: the join can only rise, and the meet can only rise as well. It is the licence for step-by-step comparisons of lattice expressions. It also lets you compare two expressions without listing every element of L.

A sublattice is a nonempty subset S of L such that for all a,b∈S, a∨b∈S and a∧b∈S. The operations are computed in L, not in S. S inherits the order from L. If S is closed under both operations, S is itself a lattice under the inherited order.

items: Take any a,b∈S and compute a∨b and a∧b in L.
Reject S if either result is outside S; accept only when both stay inside for every pair.

blocks.text: A subposet is any subset of L with the inherited order; it need not be closed. Every sublattice is a subposet, but not every subposet is a sublattice.

Bounded case: if L has least element 0 and greatest element 1, a bounded sublattice that keeps the same bounds must contain 0 and 1. A sublattice can have its own 0 and 1 different from L; then it is not a bounded sublattice of L in the same sense. See Chapter 5.4 for bounded lattices. Some syllabi write sub-lattice.

examples.question: In A={1,2,3,4,6,12} ordered by divisibility, test S={1,2,4,12} and T={1,2,3,12} for being sublattices. Show the needed joins and meets.
steps: In divisibility order, x≤y means x divides y. So a∨b=lcm(a,b) and a∧b=gcd(a,b).
With the least element 1, 1∨x=x and 1∧x=1 for every x in S. Equal pairs are covered by idempotence. Every result lies in S, and S is nonempty, so S is a sublattice.
For T, 2∨3=lcm(2,3)=6. The value 6 is not in T, so T is not closed under join and is not a sublattice. T is still a subposet because it inherits the divisibility order.
examples.answer: S={1,2,4,12} is a sublattice; T={1,2,3,12} is not, because 2∨3=6 leaves T.
examples.check:
from math import gcd
def lcm(a,b):
    return a*b//gcd(a,b)
print(lcm(2,4))
print(gcd(2,4))
print(lcm(4,12))
print(gcd(4,12))
print(lcm(2,12))
print(gcd(2,12))
print(lcm(2,3))

traps: Checking closure under only join or only meet. A sublattice must stay inside S under both operations.
Computing join and meet inside S after deleting elements. Compute them in the parent lattice L; the result may fall outside S.
Treating any nonempty subset as a sublattice. A subposet only inherits the order; it need not be closed.
Forgetting the nonempty condition. Under this definition the empty set is not a sublattice.
For a bounded sublattice, forgetting to keep the same 0 and 1 as the parent lattice when the bounds must be preserved.

quiz.q: State the idempotent, commutative, associative and absorption identities of a lattice.
quiz.a: a∨a=a and a∧a=a; a∨b=b∨a and a∧b=b∧a; (a∨b)∨c=a∨(b∨c) and (a∧b)∧c=a∧(b∧c); a∨(a∧b)=a and a∧(a∨b)=a.

quiz.q: Why is a∨a=a in a lattice defined by order?
quiz.a: The set {a,a} is just {a}. Its least upper bound is a, so a∨a=a.

quiz.q: In A={1,2,3,4,6,12} under divisibility, test S={1,2,4,12}. Give two sample computations.
quiz.a: 2∨4=lcm(2,4)=4 and 4∧12=gcd(4,12)=4, both in S. All pairs stay in S, so S is a sublattice.

quiz.q: For T={1,2,3,12} in the same A, find one join or meet that leaves T.
quiz.a: 2∨3=lcm(2,3)=6, and 6∉T. So T is not closed under join.

quiz.q: A nonempty subset S of a lattice is closed under join. Does it follow that S is a sublattice? Explain.
quiz.a: No. In the Boolean lattice on {00,01,10,11}, S={01,10,11} is closed under join, but 01∧10=00∉S. Meet closure is also required.

quiz.q: Give one difference between a subposet and a sublattice.
quiz.a: A subposet only inherits the order. A sublattice must also be nonempty and closed under join and meet.

quiz.q: Why must a bounded sublattice contain the same 0 and 1 as the parent lattice if it is to keep the bounds?
quiz.a: The least and greatest elements are part of the bounded structure. If 0 or 1 is missing, the subset may have different bounds or no bounds from the parent.

beyond: Not for the exam. Closure under join and meet is the same idea as closure under lcm and gcd in number theory. Programming languages use finite lattices in data-flow analysis, where every merge point must produce a value inside the chosen domain. Search for Galois connection, closure operator and data-flow lattice to see the next step. Bounded sublattices reappear in formal concept analysis and in type systems with top and bottom types.
